OpenAI cuts out SpaceX-owned Cursor

PLUS: Submit your iOS app to the App Store with Codex

Zach Mink

August 31, 2026

Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Visit sabrina.dev

Good morning, AI enthusiasts, and welcome to our 9,208 new readers. Sam Altman and Elon Musk have fought over companies, lawsuits, talent, and more. Now the feud is landing somewhere developers may actually feel it… One of the most popular AI coding editors on the market.

OpenAI's models will exit the newly SpaceX-owned Cursor by mid-November, with Musk's record on past agreements as the dealbreaker. Elon’s response? He “couldn’t care less.”

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI & CURSOR

✂️ OpenAI cuts out Cursor after SpaceX acquisition

Image source: Images 2.0 / The Rundown

The Rundown: OpenAI just announced that it will be removing its models from coding platform Cursor by Nov.12, coming after the company was acquired by SpaceX last month — citing Elon Musk’s history of violating contracts as the reason for the decision.

The details:

  • OAI said it stretched the wind-down as far as its contract allows via cancellation rights that opened once Cursor was sold, calling the decision “incredibly tough.”

  • OAI's evidence includes the $2M-a-year tweet deal Musk killed after buying Twitter, plus xAI training on its outputs, which Musk called “partly” true.

  • Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown reaffirmed support for Cursor, with many calling out the company’s similar move against Windsurf over its potential OAI acquisition.

  • Musk posted “I couldn't care less,” while Cursor CEO Michael Truell pushed for a fix, putting OAI's slice of its AI traffic at a seemingly light 5% of overall usage.

Why it matters: Cursor has typically been a neutral coding editor carrying all frontier options for developers to choose from. Now, it finds itself in the middle of the lunchroom fight between Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Though with xAI’s newfound Grok surge and Cursor’s internal model progress, competition might also play a bigger role than ever.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE

💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Zach, Editor-in-chief: It’s one of my favorite times of the year… Fantasy football draft season! But I was feeling particularly behind on my research this year, and my first draft that snuck up on me was a keeper league that complicates the structure and player pool.

I used Claude to help build a war room plan for the draft, dropping in our league settings, keepers, and a brain dump of my ideal strategies and gut reads. After a few clarifying questions, Claude went out to research and came back a few minutes later with a generated live artifact based on its scan. The strategy factored in my exact pick slots and expected available players, potential targets built around my keepers, and (admittedly) sharp rationales for some options I hadn’t considered.

Once in the draft, I updated my picks as they went, and Claude then modified the page, recalibrating ideal options based on where my team was trending. Highly recommend as a co-manager!

Adrian, Developer: A while ago, my dad told me he wanted to use AI to analyze matches for the World Cup. He had never coded before, and his AI experience was pretty much limited to occasionally asking Gemini a question. I installed Claude Code for him and gave him a few prompting tips. He ended up building a full football analytics site himself and putting it on Vercel so he could show it off to his friends.

Getting started with AI is much easier than people assume; sometimes you just need a project you actually want to make. Now that the Premier League season has kicked off, he's already reworking the site for that.

📱 Submit your iOS app to the App Store with Codex

Visit The Rundown University

The Rundown: In this guide, you will learn how to take a mobile app from Xcode to the App Store with ChatGPT Work and App Store Connect. You will prepare the listing, upload the build, set a price, and submit it without hunting through every screen.

Step-by-step:

  1. Start with a working app. Follow Part 1 to build it. Tell Codex: “Build this app and send it to App Store Connect.” It will build, archive, and distribute it from Xcode

  2. Open App Store Connect in Codex's browser and sign in. Tell Codex to fill the description, upload screenshots of the app, and everything else needed

  3. Complete the App Review contact, age-rating, and content-rights fields, then select the build. Review each answer before continuing

  4. Set a price in App Store Connect, then click "Add for Review". You may see flags for things that need to be fixed. Fix each, then click "Submit for Review"

Pro tip: If you want a subscription or one-time premium upgrade, ask Codex to add Apple’s StoreKit framework, then set up the product in App Store Connect.

ANTHROPIC VS. DEPARTMENT OF WAR

👨🏻‍⚖️ Court rejects Pentagon's Anthropic blacklist

Image source: Court Listener

The Rundown: A federal judge ruled that the Pentagon broke the law when it blacklisted Anthropic as a “supply chain risk,” deciding that it was payback for the lab's pushback on military AI rather than a response to a real security threat.

The details:

  • The Dept. of War issued the label in June, forcing its frontier Mythos and Fable models offline for nearly a month while the two sides publicly sparred.

  • The move made Anthropic the first U.S. firm ever hit with a designation typically reserved for foreign adversaries, with all govt. agencies ordered to drop its models.

  • Judge Rita Lin held that the blacklist violated the First and Fifth Amendments, saying national security isn’t a “blank check” to punish critics.

  • The label still technically survives while a second case sits in appeals court, and the Pentagon has said its “wind down” of Claude usage will finish by Sept. 30.

Why it matters: Anthropic scores the ruling confirming what many in the industry felt (including ourselves) in June — that the label was more retaliatory than safety-related. While Anthropic might no longer have the Pentagon as a customer regardless, future attempts to block models may now come with a legal precedent for pushback.

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Zan built a local Publisher-to-PDF converter

Today’s workflow comes from reader Zan:

Microsoft is retiring Publisher on Oct. 1, 2026. I have many .PUB files that I need to convert to PDFs before then, but I did not want to use online converters. I wanted a solution that would run locally on my computer.

I worked with Claude to create a lightweight program that searches for .PUB files on a drive of my choice and converts them into high-quality PDF files, placing each new PDF in the same folder as its source file.

Opening PowerShell manually and managing permissions was too cumbersome, so Claude also created a batch file to make the process easier. For anyone who wants to create their own mini-program, I asked Claude to create a reusable prompt.
